Plotting actors per normalisation¶

In [11]:
medians_rel = median_widths / median_widths.mean()

long = medians_rel.melt(var_name="normalisation", value_name="relative_width")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.axhline(1, color="grey", linestyle="--", linewidth=1, zorder=0)
sns.stripplot(data=long, x="normalisation", y="relative_width", jitter=0.12, size=7, alpha=0.75, color="tab:blue", ax=ax)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(cv)))
ax.set_xticklabels([f"{name}\nCV = {value:.3f}" for name, value in cv["CV"].items()])
ax.set_xlabel("")
ax.set_ylabel("Median mouth width / mean over actors")
ax.set_title("Neutral mouth width per actor, relative to the mean")
sns.despine(ax=ax)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The "raw" and "image" columns show the same spread, while the "inter-ocular" column shows a much tighter spread.

Answer to Q2.1¶

Normalisation¶

Inter-ocular distance¶

Leaves less variation between actors, the coefficient of variation of the 20 median neutral mouth widths is 0.046, against 0.079 for the normalisation by the image dimensions

The distance d is computed in each frame and scales with the apparent size of the face, so dividing by it expresses every coordinate in units of the inter-ocular distance. Actors such as 5 and 11 have wide mouths in pixels but are close to the mean once divided by d. The variation that remains reflects real differences in facial proportions between people, which is good since it is what a normalisation should achieve.

Image normalisation¶

Does not reduce the variation at all, its CV is practically the same as raw. The CV is a ratio of standard deviation to mean, so dividing every actor by the same constants leaves it unchanged. The small difference comes only from x and y being divided by different constants. Actors still differ in how large their face appears in the image, because of their distance to the camera and the size of their head.

Dividing x by 1280 and y by 720 also distorts the geometry of the face. The two axes are scaled by different factors, so the face is stretched vertically by 1280/720 ≈ 1.78 relative to its width. A distance then depends on its orientation, angles are not preserved, and tilting the head changes the measurements. The result also depends on the resolution of the camera.

All the remaining tasks use the normalisation by d.

Outlier density per coordinate and emotion¶

Statistics (Q1, Q3, mean, std) computed within the frames of each emotion, one coordinate at a time.

In [13]:
coords = norm.X_COLS + norm.Y_COLS  # all 136 normalised coordinates

# same signature for the three rules, so the loop can call them the same way
rules = {
    "IQR": lambda X: outl.iqr_flags(X),
    "z (k=3)": lambda X: outl.zscore_flags(X, 3),
    "z (k=4)": lambda X: outl.zscore_flags(X, 4),
}

density = {}
for rule, flag in rules.items():
    rows = {}
    for code, name in cfg.EMOTIONS.items():
        X = df_d.loc[df_d["emotion"] == code, coords]  # frames of this emotion only
        rows[name] = 100 * flag(X).mean(axis=0) # ro for each coordinate
    table = pd.DataFrame(rows, index=coords).T # emotions x coordinates
    table["mean"] = table[coords].mean(axis=1)
    table["std"] = table[coords].std(axis=1, ddof=0)
    density[rule] = table

Answer to Q2.2¶

The quartiles, the mean and the standard deviation are computed within the frames of each emotion, so ρ measures how many frames are atypical for that emotion, not how much the face moves in it.

In every emotion the IQR flags more frames than the z-score with k = 3, and k = 3 more than k = 4: the mean ρ ranges from 0.7 % to 3.9 % with the IQR, from 0.2 % to 0.9 % with k = 3 and from 0.01 % to 0.3 % with k = 4. This follows from how the rules are built: even for normal data without anomalies, Tukey's fences lie at about ±2.7σ and flag about 0.7 % of the values, against 0.27 % for |z| > 3 and 0.006 % for |z| > 4. Neutral is close to these references, while the other emotions are above them for all three rules, so extreme values are more frequent than in a normal distribution. The two rules also differ in robustness: the quartiles are not affected by the extreme values, while the mean and the standard deviation are pulled and inflated by them, so the z-score can hide the outliers it is looking for.

Between emotions, neutral has the lowest density for all three rules, and angry and disgust are always in the upper half. The ranking is not the same for every rule: calm has the highest mean ρ with the IQR (3.9 %) but is seventh of eight with both z-scores, so the rules do not always agree on which emotion has the most outliers. Finally, the standard deviation of ρ is of the same order as its mean, or larger, in every emotion and rule: the density depends strongly on the coordinate, and the mean over the 136 coordinates summarises it only roughly.

Q 2.3.¶

In [17]:
sad = df_d[df_d["emotion"] == 4].copy()  # sad frames only

# new column: True if y_57 is outside the IQR fences
sad["flag"] = outl.iqr_flags(sad[["y_57"]])[:, 0]  # [[...]] = 1-column matrix, [:, 0] = back to a vector

sad["side"] = np.where(sad["y_57"] < sad["y_57"].median(), "low", "high")

flagged = sad[sad["flag"]]  # True/False mask - keep flagged rows
In [18]:
by_actor = pd.crosstab(flagged["actor"], flagged["side"])  # count flagged frames per actor and side
# all actors of sad (0 if none flagged), columns in a fixed order
by_actor = by_actor.reindex(index=sorted(sad["actor"].unique()), columns=["low", "high"], fill_value=0)
# number of different videos the flagged frames come from
by_actor["videos"] = flagged.groupby("actor")["video_id"].nunique().reindex(by_actor.index, fill_value=0)
# share of the actor's sad frames that are flagged
by_actor["%"] = 100 * by_actor[["low", "high"]].sum(axis=1) / sad.groupby("actor").size()
by_actor.round(1)

Answer to Q2.3¶

We study y_57 (lower edge of the lower lip) in sad with the IQR rule: y_57 is the variable of 2.5 to 2.8, sad has flagged frames on both sides of its box in 2.2, and the IQR flags exactly the points drawn beyond the whiskers.

The 220 flagged frames (1.25 %) come from 10 actors and 25 videos, but they are concentrated: actor 21 alone has 124, and actors 21 and 20 about three quarters. No video has flagged frames on both sides of the box, and those below it come only from actors 20, 15 and 11.

None of the three videos examined shows isolated jumps. For actor 21, y_57 rises and falls smoothly above the fence at full confidence, and only the mouth and the chin change: a wide-open mouth, a legitimate expression. The flagged frames of actor 20 lie just below the fence, also at full confidence. In both cases the face of the actor explains much of it: the median y_57 of each actor in sad follows its median in neutral, with actor 21 and actors 20 and 11 at the extremes in both, a difference in face shape that the normalisation by d does not remove (2.1). Actor 15 is the exception: in its last ten frames y_57 falls from about 0.9 to 0.5 d as the head bends down, the confidence drops as the fall begins, and the lips collapse near the nose, so these frames do not describe the expression.

The flagged frames are kept, neither removed nor corrected. Almost all of them are legitimate, and removing them would mainly discard the strongest expressions and penalise a few actors. The one problematic case was found by inspecting a video by hand, which cannot be applied as a rule to the test actors or to the application, and the confidence is back to 0.98 in its most extreme frames, so it cannot serve as that rule either. Its effect on the features of that video is a limitation.

Answer to Q2.4¶

k-means is applied to (x_54, y_54) of all development frames, with the eight emotions together and without scaling: both coordinates are in units of d, so the distance to a centroid is a real distance on the face. For the comparison with 2.2, the IQR rule is applied to the same frames, flagging a frame outside the fences in x_54 or in y_54.

The IQR flags far more frames than k-means (6.4 % against 1.2 % to 1.9 %). The cloud of points is diagonal, the mouth corner moving up as it moves out, and the rectangle formed by the fences cannot follow it: the dense ends of the diagonal lie outside it and are flagged. With k = 2, k-means flags the outer border of the cloud and is almost a subset of the IQR (99.5 % of its flagged frames). With more clusters it adapts to the shape: clusters cover the ends of the diagonal, which are no longer flagged, while the small, tight clusters of the centre flag normal frames at their edges. With k = 8, more than half of the flagged frames are not flagged by the IQR, and the number of flagged frames does not fall steadily with k = (2554, 1603, 1673). All methods flag the trails of points that leave the cloud, which look like consecutive frames of single videos, as the head movement of actor 15 in 2.3.

On a random sample of 2000 frames, DBSCAN (min_samples = 4) finds one main cluster and a few small ones at its border, and the noise depends strongly on eps: from 111 frames with 0.015 to 14 with 0.03, all three values used were within the elbow of the k-distance plot. The larger eps, the more the noise coincides with the IQR (75 % to 86 %). Something that needs to be noted is that the trails do not appear in the sample, so the result on the sample may differ from the result on all frames.

Answer to Q2.6¶

With k = 3, the z-score flags 1597 frames, 974 of which were injected. Recall is 0.368: it finds 974 of the 2644 injected frames. Precision is 0.610: 974 of the 1597 flagged frames were injected.

Recall is low for two reasons. First, none of the 1335 values injected with s = −1 is detected. q is added on both sides, so on this side it pulls the value back towards the mean, and these values end up between 2 and 3 standard deviations below it, where |z| ≤ 3.

Second, only 974 of the 1309 values injected with s = +1 are detected. They were placed between 3 and 4 standard deviations above the mean of the clean variable, but the detector computes the mean and the standard deviation on the contaminated variable, where the injected values themselves raise the standard deviation from 0.0748 to 0.0808. Measured with this larger standard deviation, every value is fewer standard deviations from the mean, and those placed closest to 3 fall below z = 3: the right red block of the 2.6 histogram crosses the +3 line. This is the masking effect: the outliers hide themselves by inflating the standard deviation.

Precision is not higher because 623 frames that were not injected also have |z| > 3: the gray tail of the histogram, real extreme values of y_57 like those traced in 2.3. Looking at one variable alone, the z-score cannot tell them apart from injected values.

A smaller k does not solve the problem: it raises recall but lowers precision. k = 2 finds 2454 injected frames (recall 0.928) but also flags 4409 frames that were not injected (precision 0.358); k = 1.5 finds all 2644 at the cost of 11 820 false positives (precision 0.183). A smaller k trades missed outliers for false alarms.

Answer to Q2.7¶

The modified z-score of the residuals flags 2736 frames, 2638 were really injected. Recall is 0.998: it misses only 6 of the 2644 injected frames. Precision is 0.964: 98 of the flagged frames were not injected. Unlike in 2.6, both sides are detected: 1330 of 1335 with s = −1 and 1308 of 1309 with s = +1.

It succeeds where 2.6 fails because it judges each value against a different reference. The z-score of 2.6 compares y_57 with the values of all the other frames, and an injected value with s = −1 is an ordinary value there. The residual compares y_57 with what its own neighbours predict in the same frame: y_57 is about the average of y_56 and y_58 (coefficients close to 0.5), and the injection changes y_57 but not its neighbours. In the scatter plot, the frames that were not injected lie along the diagonal, and the injected ones form two horizontal bands far from it.

The same reasoning reduces the false positives from 623 in 2.6 to 98. The real extreme frames are extreme in y_57, but their neighbours move with them, so their residual is usually small: in the scatter plot, the frames with the lowest and highest y_57 continue along the diagonal.

A robust threshold is needed because the injected frames have very large residuals, and these inflate the standard deviation of the residuals to 0.0335, against 0.0030 for MAD / 0.6745. With the plain z-score a residual has to be 0.117 away from the centre to be flagged; with the modified z-score is 0.0106. The plain z-score of the same residuals misses 294 injected frames (recall 0.889) because of the masking effect of 2.6 again. The median and the MAD are not pulled by the outliers.

The 6 missed frames are injected values that happen to be close to the prediction, where the red bands cross the diagonal. The 98 false positives are frames that were not injected but differ from the prediction by more than 0.0106. This is the cost of the narrower cutoff: the plain z-score of the residuals, with a much wider cutoff, has no false positives (precision 1.000).

Answer to Q2.8¶

The regression (b) is the best replacement, with a mean absolute error of 0.0021 at the injected positions, followed by the linear interpolation (a), with 0.0045, and the mean (c), with 0.0580.

The regression uses the neighbouring landmarks, 56 and 58, in the same frame. 2.7 showed that y_57 follows them closely: it is about their average (coefficients close to 0.5), and the frames that were not injected lie along the diagonal of the scatter plot. In the figure, the squares of (b) fall on the original curve.

The interpolation uses the neighbouring frames, the same landmark 57 in the valid frames before and after. It comes close, but it assumes that y_57 changes in a straight line between those frames: when the lip changes direction or speed within that interval, or when the interval is longer (several consecutive flagged frames, or the first or last frame of a video, where the nearest value is copied), the estimate departs from the original.

The mean is by far the worst, about 13 times the error of (a) and 28 times that of (b). It puts the same value in every flagged frame, whatever the frame, the video or the expression: in the figure, the triangles stay at 0.99 while the original curve is between 1.0 and 1.1.

If the neighbouring landmarks had failed in the same frames, the regression would predict y_57 from wrong values of y_56 and y_58, so it could no longer be trusted. The interpolation would then be the choice, because it only needs y_57 itself in the neighbouring frames.
